chapter_theme: An urging to virtue: human birth is rare and the body brief, so its fruit, virtue, must be gathered now. Those who live on the merit of past births without adding to it end at others' gates; those who have gathered it face death without grief, and even a small gift to the worthy grows vast.
structure_note: The chapter turns between the consequences of neglecting virtue (31-33), the body as a means to be used up for virtue (34-37), the growth of a small good (38), the passing of days (39) and, last, honour over a body kept alive by begging (40).

31.reading: Those who, on the strength of earlier austerity, do no austerity now will look up at a house and say 'those inside are the ones who live', unable to enter, clinging to the outer door and grieving.
31.nuance: The quatrain implies merit is a stock that is used up: present comfort is paid for by past austerity, and without renewal the next state is the beggar's at the gate. Pope's main text reads the cause as a lack of former penance, but his bracketed note agrees with Shanmuganar that past penance won their present state.

positions.position: Those who enjoyed the fruit of past virtue and do none in this birth will stand outside in their next birth.

32.reading: Base heart, which says 'let us prosper, desiring wealth and forgetting virtue', even if you live on toiling without rest, your days are gone: tell me what you will do.
32.nuance: The address is to one's own heart (புலைநெஞ்சே), and the closing question is left unanswered; the speaker is arguing with himself.

33.reading: When the fruit of past deeds arrives, the fool sighs hotly and his mind breaks; those who think of what comes as old desert pass beyond the bounds of confusion and are freed.
33.nuance: Accepting suffering as the ripening of one's own past deeds is presented as the way out of the round itself, not only as consolation. Pope's 'by devoting themselves to virtue' is his addition.

34.reading: With the gain of having obtained this rare body, take its great fruit fully; like juice pressed from cane, it serves you afterwards, and the body goes like the crushed refuse.
34.nuance: The body is valued only as the cane is: for what can be pressed out of it. The juice, virtue, outlasts the body and is what helps 'afterwards'.

35.reading: As those who crushed their cane and took the jaggery early do not grieve when the refuse catches fire and burns, those who laboured to take the body's fruit feel no distress when Death comes.
35.nuance: சிறுகாலை (early) carries the argument: the jaggery was made in time. The burning of refuse quietly suggests cremation.

36.reading: Without asking whether it is today, that day or some other day, think that Death stands right behind you; leave evil as far as you can and hold to the virtue the worthy practise.
36.nuance: ஒல்லும் வகையால் (as far as you can) sets a measure within reach, unlike the absolute demands of renunciation elsewhere in these chapters.

37.reading: If the gains that come through human birth are many when examined, one should not live doing service only to the gathered-up body, but should act so as to enjoy them in the world above.
37.nuance: The verse applies ஒப்புரவு, normally service to the community, to the body itself, ironically: serving the body is a misplaced kind of duty.

38.reading: As a banyan seed of the smallest size grows and casts a vast shade, so the fruit of virtue, though small, when it reaches the hands of the worthy, spreads so that the sky seems small.
38.nuance: The growth depends on the recipient: தக்கார் கைப்பட்டக்கால் (if it falls into worthy hands). Pope reads உறக்கும் துணைய as 'minute as one might see in dreams'; Shanmuganar renders the size differently, but both make the seed tiny.

39.reading: Seeing day follow day, they do not grasp it, and rejoice each day that the day will pass well; they do not count each passing day as a day taken from their own lives.
39.nuance: The quatrain plays வைகல் (day; passing) through eight forms, so the sound of repetition becomes the experience it describes. Mudaliar reports another reading of வைகுதல் as 'staying', and supplies the unstated conclusion: the wise would act on virtue at once.

40.reading: I would put off the rare jewel of honour and live by the shame of begging, if a body fed by such disgrace would gain strength and last.
40.nuance: The conditional is counterfactual: the body will not last, so honour is never worth selling for it. Mudaliar notes the particle மன் signals exactly this unfulfilled 'I would'.

links.note: Both read present fortune as the visible fruit of virtue: the Kural's palanquin rider and bearer, the Naladiyar's insider and the one at the gate. The Naladiyar adds that the insider's place is lost when the merit is not renewed.
Kural 32 says no ruin exceeds forgetting virtue (மறத்தல்); this quatrain stages the heart that forgets virtue (அறமறந்து) for wealth and asks it what it will do now.
Both make the arrival of past deeds' fruit an occasion for equanimity; the Naladiyar goes further and makes that acceptance the way out of rebirth's confusion.
Both use crushed sugar-cane. In the Kural the base yield only when crushed, a reproach; here the body should be crushed for its juice, a counsel.
Both say virtue gathered in time stays when the body perishes; the Kural calls it an undying companion, the Naladiyar the jaggery kept when the cane refuse burns.
Both turn on not knowing when death comes: the Kural mocks those who plan crores of things without knowing they will live another moment, and this quatrain answers with Death standing behind.
22 urges ஒப்புரவு before one's days end; 37 warns against an ஒப்புரவு done only for the body. Together they mark the word's proper object as others, not oneself.

Both make a small good large: the Kural's millet-sized help counted as a palmyra by those who know its worth, the Naladiyar's banyan seed. The Naladiyar places the growth in the worthiness of the recipient.
Kural 334 says the day looks like a thing but is a saw cutting life, to those who see it; this quatrain describes those who do not see it, and rejoice at each day.

Both argue that keeping the body alive at the cost of dignity buys nothing, since the body does not last: the Kural asks if it is a medicine, the Naladiyar makes the bargain conditional on a body that never dies.

new_concepts.gloss: the body, as a perishable and impure frame
new_concepts.label_source: The verses use யாக்கை (18, 27, 28, 30, 34) and the chapter title யாக்கை நிலையாமை.

source_issues: Quatrains 31-38: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned.
Quatrain 31: the Tamil reads பறங்கடை, apparently for புறங்கடை (outer door), as Shanmuganar's வெளிக்கடைவாயில் and Pope's 'outer gate' suggest.
Quatrain 37: the Tamil has two apparent misprints, பொரும்பயனும் for பெரும்பயனும் and ஒப்புராவு for ஒப்புரவு.
Quatrain 40: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
